name: Jade Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Jade, thanks for making the time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you say here is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the little express supermarket by the train station, the chain one. I start at six, so the first three hours are commuters, coffee from the machine, meal deals, newspapers, all very fast. After nine it's restocking the sandwich fridge, checking dates and doing the till for the school mums and pensioners.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the morning rush, honestly, it's like a dance once you get it, though I still mess up the coffee machine and the meal deal codes. What wears me out is being on the lowest pay and getting told off by the area manager for things like the fridge layout. Some days I think I could run the place better, other days I can't find the milk delivery note.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Luc, he's a plumber's apprentice. I bake celebration cakes at weekends and sell them through social media, birthdays, christenings, that sort of thing, it was my nan's recipe book that started it. I use AI every day for the cake business, pricing, captions, replying to orders, it's brilliant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So AI's just a helper. That's already what it is for me, so not much changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy for small businesses and nothing to be scared of. At work I'd show the girls how to use it for their own stuff. Online I'd keep posting my cakes with AI-written captions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the shop job stays the same low pay with under a month saved. The cakes bring in maybe a hundred and fifty a month, which is what stops us going overdrawn. I want to grow that, because I don't want to be on the till at thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a second-hand stand mixer this winter, about a hundred and twenty, so I can do more orders. I'd ask the store to put me on the earlier shift permanently, so I've got afternoons for baking. I'd look into the food hygiene rating so I can sell to cafés, not just birthdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, a bit impatient. Like I'm on the starting line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if the mixer stretched you too far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Going out with friends on Fridays, and my nails, I'd do them myself. Luc would complain about no takeaways. It's fine, my nan raised four kids on less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why don't you want to be on the till at thirty-five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to build something of my own, like my nan did with her bakery. Working for a big chain is fine for now. A big chain would replace me tomorrow if it saved a penny, and that's their right, but I don't have to stay.

say: AI is **handy** for small businesses and nothing to be **scared of**.
I'd show the girls at work how to use it for **their own stuff**.
think: The shop job stays **low pay** with under a month saved.
My cakes bring in about **a hundred and fifty** a month.
do: Buy a **second-hand stand mixer** this winter for about a hundred and twenty.
Ask for a permanent **early shift** to free afternoons for baking.
Get a **food hygiene rating** to sell to cafés.
S0.quote: A big chain would replace me tomorrow if it saved a penny, and that's their right, but I don't have to stay.
fieldNote: Her **cake business** already keeps the couple out of overdraft.
Accepts the **chain's right** to cut costs, and plans her exit instead of complaining.
Draws on her **nan's bakery** as a model of building something of her own.

steps.text: Buy a second-hand stand mixer this winter
Ask for a permanent early shift to free afternoons
Get a food hygiene rating to sell cakes to cafés
Do her own nails and skip Friday nights out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first, answering customers, booking, buying. That's half my cake business, and I already use AI for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small businesses win from this, because one person can now do what took three. At work I'd say the shop floor's fine for a few years. I'd tell people to learn the tools while they're cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think this is my chance. The AI takes the boring bits of the cake business, orders, invoices, replies, so I can bake more. The shop job is hands-on, so robots come later, which gives me a few years of steady wage while I grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI to set up proper online ordering with a calendar and deposits in the first three months. I'd aim to supply two cafés in town with traybakes by next summer. I'd keep the shop job full time for now, because I can't risk the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit nervous about doing it all on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pat, the supervisor, she's mostly paperwork and ordering and the area manager's emails. If the AI does that, she's got nothing left but the till. She's been good to me, I'd want to help her find something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You trust AI for your business. Do you worry it'll compete with you too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for cakes, a machine can't taste my nan's lemon drizzle. Maybe later with robots in factories, but people want handmade for christenings. I think the personal touch is the last thing to go.

I'd tell people to **learn the tools** while they're cheap.
think: AI takes the **boring bits** of the cake business so I can bake more.
The shop job is **hands-on**, giving a few years of steady wage.
do: Set up **online ordering** with deposits in three months, using AI.
Supply **two cafés** with traybakes by next summer.
Keep the shop job **full time** for the rent.
feel: Mostly **excited**, a bit **nervous** doing it alone.
S1.quote: A machine can't taste my nan's lemon drizzle.
fieldNote: Sees Steady Disruption as **opportunity**: AI does her admin so she can bake.
Worries for **Pat**, a supervisor whose day is mostly paperwork.
Keeps the **wage** as a safety net despite her confidence.

steps.text: Set up online cake ordering with deposits using AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, then robots in 2031. Wow. That's a lot faster than I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a time for families to pull together and for people to make things themselves. I'd tell people to start a small business, not wait for the government. Online I'd probably share how I'm using AI to survive it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the shop job goes by 2031, and before that the chain will cut hours as AI plans everything. My cake business might do well for a bit, but if everyone loses their jobs, who's buying birthday cakes? That's what scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the cakes hard this year, aiming for four hundred a month, and get a small bank loan for a proper oven if the numbers work. Luc would finish his plumbing apprenticeship, because robots in people's lofts feel far off. We'd move the wedding money into the business and get married at the registry office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but fired up. It's like my nan in the war, you make do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't a loan a big risk with less than a month saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it is, and I'd only do it with orders already booked. Nan always said never borrow for something you can't sell. I'd want three months of orders in the diary first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your nan about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm doing what she did, baking our way through hard times. She'd tell me to keep my shop job as long as they'll have me. She was always the sensible one.

say: It's a time for **families to pull together** and make things themselves.
I'd tell people to start a **small business**, not wait for government.
think: The shop job goes by **2031**, with hours cut before that.
If everyone loses their jobs, who's buying **birthday cakes**?
do: Grow the cakes to **four hundred** a month this year.
Take a small **bank loan** for an oven, only with orders booked.
Move the **wedding money** into the business.
feel: **Scared** but **fired up**, making do like her nan.
S2.quote: If everyone loses their jobs, who's buying birthday cakes?
fieldNote: Expects to **lose the shop job** and sees her side business depending on others' wages.
Cautious about debt: a loan only with **three months** of orders booked.
Her partner's **plumbing** apprenticeship becomes the household anchor.

steps.text: Grow cake sales to four hundred a month this year
Take a small bank loan for an oven once orders are booked
Marry at the registry office and move wedding money to the business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AGI and robots by 2034. Better. I could actually build something in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for anyone willing to work for it. I'd tell the younger girls at the shop to learn a craft or a trade. Online I'd share how I'm growing the cake business step by step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have till about 2034 on the till, seven years, and that's enough to build the cakes into a proper business. The worry is still whether people have money to spend. If half the town loses office jobs in 2031, my orders drop too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the food hygiene rating this year, the second-hand mixer, and two café contracts by 2028. I'd go part-time at the shop once the cakes bring in five hundred a month, not before. Luc and I would marry in church in 2028 as we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a little knot about money. Five years feels like enough if I don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why five hundred a month before you go part-time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's half my shop wage, and that covers my share of the rent. Under that, I'd be gambling. My nan said pay the rent first, dream second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No loan, because I'd have time to save for the oven. And a proper church wedding, because I don't want to rush that. Time changes everything about the plan.

say: There's time for anyone **willing to work** for it.
I'd tell younger girls at the shop to learn a **craft or trade**.
think: Seven years on the till is enough to build a **proper business**.
If **office jobs** go in 2031, my orders drop too.
do: Go **part-time** at the shop only at five hundred a month from cakes.
S3.quote: My nan said pay the rent first, dream second.
fieldNote: Expects the shop job to go by 2034 but feels **in control** of her exit.
Sets a clear threshold, **five hundred** a month, before cutting shop hours.
With five years she drops the **loan** and keeps the church wedding.

steps.text: Win two café contracts for traybakes by 2028
Cut to part-time once cakes earn five hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots around 2039. That's plenty of time. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a gift, and anyone who's caught out wasn't paying attention. I'd tell people to start their own thing slowly. Online I'd keep showing how AI helps small sellers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think by 2036 I could have my own little shop, like my nan's, with AI doing the books and orders. The shop job would just be a memory. The only thing that worries me is whether people in town still have money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the cake business steadily, café contracts first, then a market stall, then maybe a small unit by 2030. I'd save every spare bit for three months of cushion first. I'd keep the express shop job until the cakes earn more than it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish, really. Excited about having time to do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your shop look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small, on the high street, cakes and bread and coffee, with my nan's photo on the wall. AI would do the ordering and the accounts, and I'd do the baking and the talking. Maybe one helper on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the robots can bake by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd sell the handmade story, because that's what people pay for at christenings. A factory cake is already cheaper than mine and people still come to me. That won't change overnight.

say: Ten years is **a gift**; anyone caught out wasn't **paying attention**.
I'd tell people to start **their own thing** slowly.
think: By 2036 I could have **my own shop**, like my nan's.
My only worry is whether people in town still have **money**.
do: Grow from **café contracts** to a market stall, then a **small unit**.
Keep the **shop job** until the cakes earn more.
S4.quote: A factory cake is already cheaper than mine and people still come to me.
fieldNote: Sees the decade as a **gift** and plans a high street shop with AI doing admin.
Her one worry is **local spending power**, not her own skills.
Bets on the **handmade story** even when robots can bake.

steps.text: Open a small cake and bread unit by 2030
Save three months of costs before leaving the shop
Use AI to run ordering and accounts for the bakery
Keep the express shop job until cakes earn more

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd lose the shop job before the cakes could carry us, and people would stop buying treats. What would help is small business loans with low interest for people like me, and cheap market stalls in town. Not handouts, just a fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people would build if they had the time. Everyone asks what we'd lose. My nan built a bakery from nothing, and I think a lot of us could do something like that with a bit of help.

headlineQuote: My nan built a bakery from nothing, and I think a lot of us could do something like that with a bit of help.
portrait: Jade is 27, working the **early shift** at an express supermarket by the train station.
She lives with **Luc**, a plumber's apprentice, and sells **celebration cakes** from her nan's recipes.
She uses **AI daily** for her side business and sees it as a helper for small sellers.
She's **self-reliant**, cautious about debt, and her plans grow bolder as the timeline lengthens.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the shop job would go before the **cakes** could carry them.
whatWouldHelp: **Low-interest loans** for small businesses and cheap **market stalls** in town.
